topic: Breath series 5: Diaphragmatic (belly) breathing (animated, guided, research)
caption:
One hand on your chest, one on your belly: which one moves when you breathe?

Belly (diaphragmatic) breathing means slow, low breaths where your belly rises more than your chest. In small studies, people who practised it regularly for a few weeks reported less stress. The research is still early.

How to try it: one hand on your belly, one on your chest. Breathe in through your nose for about four seconds, letting your belly rise, then slowly out through your nose for about six. A trial comparing a longer out-breath with an even one found no clear difference, so go at a pace that feels easy.

Keep it gentle. If you feel light-headed or tingly, go back to your usual breathing. If you have COPD or another lung condition, check with your doctor first: in some studies of people with COPD, deep belly breathing made breathing harder work.

Save this for another time.

Research:
Kwon, C.-Y. et al. (2026). The health effects of diaphragmatic breathing: A systematic review. Complement Ther Med, 96, 103317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ctim.2025.103317
Hopper, S. I. et al. (2019). Effectiveness of diaphragmatic breathing for reducing physiological and psychological stress in adults: A quantitative systematic review. JBI Database System Rev Implement Rep, 17(9), 1855-1876. https://doi.org/10.11124/JBISRIR-2017-003848
Birdee, G. et al. (2023). Slow breathing for reducing stress: The effect of extending exhale. Complement Ther Med, 73, 102937. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ctim.2023.102937
Vitacca, M. et al. (1998). Acute effects of deep diaphragmatic breathing in COPD patients with chronic respiratory insufficiency. Eur Respir J, 11(2), 408-415. https://doi.org/10.1183/09031936.98.11020408
Holland, A. E. et al. (2012). Breathing exercises for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2012(10), CD008250. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD008250.pub2
